title: Dress for the cold
summary: Wear several loose layers: a wool, silk or synthetic layer next to the skin, an insulating middle layer and a wind- and water-resistant outer layer. Skip cotton. Cover your head, face, hands and feet. Take layers off before you sweat, and change out of wet clothes.
doFirst: Wet? Change into dry clothes: wet clothing chills the body quickly (CDC, Red Cross).
Warming up while you work? Take a layer off before you sweat (CDC; Priorities).
Cover your nose, ears, cheeks, chin, fingers and toes: frostbite hits them most often (CDC).

blocks.p: Wear at least three layers of loose-fitting clothing: layering gives better insulation (OSHA). Layers create more dead air space (Army FM 21-76-1).

head: Layer
What it does
rows: Keeps moisture away from the body (OSHA)
Insulates even when wet (OSHA), by trapping air close to your body (CDC)
Protects from wind, rain and snow (CDC), and lets some air through to prevent overheating (OSHA)

list: Keep it loose: tight clothing reduces blood circulation, and warm blood needs to reach your hands and feet (OSHA).
Remember COLD: keep clothing Clean, avoid Overheating, wear it Loose and in layers, and keep it Dry (Priorities). Dirt reduces clothing’s insulation (Army FM 21-76-1).
Indoors with the heat out, the same rules apply: see Stay warm when the heat is out.

blocks.label: Stay warm when the heat is out

blocks.p: Wear fabrics that hold more body heat and don’t absorb moisture. Wool, silk or polypropylene hold more body heat than cotton (CDC, OSHA). Wear dry clothing made of wool or synthetics; avoid cotton (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research).

list: Head: a hat that covers your ears. Hats reduce the body heat that escapes from your head (OSHA, NIOSH).
Face: a scarf or knit mask over your face and mouth (CDC). Cover your mouth to protect your lungs from very cold air (Red Cross).
Hands: mittens are warmer than gloves (CDC). Sleeves should be snug at the wrist (CDC). Insulated gloves, water-resistant if needed (OSHA).
Feet: insulated, waterproof boots (OSHA, NIOSH). Keep socks dry and change them regularly (Army FM 21-76-1). Wet feet lose heat 25 times faster than dry feet (OSHA).
Carry spares: extra socks, gloves, hat, jacket, clothes and blankets (NIOSH).

blocks.p: The parts frostbite hits most often are the nose, ears, toes, cheeks, chin and fingers: keep them covered in warm, dry clothing (CDC).

sections.h: Stay dry: vent before you sweat

list: Stay dry: wet clothing chills the body quickly (CDC). Moisture, for example from sweat, increases the rate of heat loss from the body (OSHA).
Too much sweating makes your body lose more heat, so take off layers whenever you feel too warm (CDC). Take layers off before hard work so sweat doesn’t soak them (Priorities).
Try not to sweat or get too tired (CDC). Sweating can lead to a chill and hypothermia (Red Cross).
Avoid getting wet, and don’t leave any skin exposed to the cold (CDC).
Change wet clothing often to prevent losing body heat (Red Cross). Keep extra clothing, including underwear, handy in case you get wet (OSHA).
Keep clothing dry so it keeps insulating. Dry damp clothing in the sun or by a fire, and dry it before dark (Army FM 21-76-1).
Fell into water in winter: take off the wet clothing, rewarm by a fire, and finish drying the clothing by the fire (Army FM 21-76-1).
No fire: take off the clothing and get into a sleeping bag if you have one. Let the wet clothes freeze, then break the ice out of them (Army FM 21-76-1).

blocks.p: Anyone soaked and cold all over: open the Hypothermia protocol.

list: Dress babies and children warmly to go out. Several thin layers keep them dry and warm. Always remember warm boots, gloves or mittens and a hat (American Academy of Pediatrics).
For older babies and young children, the rule of thumb is one more layer of clothing than an adult would wear in the same conditions (American Academy of Pediatrics).
In the car, babies and children should wear thin, snug layers, not thick, bulky coats or snowsuits (American Academy of Pediatrics).
Wind chill tests were done on adults: be even more cautious with children (National Weather Service).

blocks.p: Babies asleep: infants under 1 year should never sleep in a cold room (CDC). Safe sleep rules for keeping a baby warm are in Stay warm when the heat is out.

blocks.label: Stay warm when the heat is out

list: Stranded with too little clothing: wrap your whole body, including your head, in extra clothing, blankets or newspapers (CDC).
To add insulation to a sleeping bag, use what you have: dry grass, leaves or dry moss (Army FM 21-76-1).
